{anvl} lowers every primitive to a StableHLO program, which XLA then compiles.
For a computation StableHLO cannot express well, XLA offers *custom calls*:
you write a C++ function, register it with the PJRT runtime under a name, and
XLA invokes it at exactly that point in the compiled program.
This article walks the whole path on CPU, and then shows what changes for
CUDA.

Everything here is specific to the **`"pjrt"` backend**.
A custom call is a handler registered with the PJRT runtime and invoked by
the XLA-compiled program, so there is nothing for {anvl}'s `quickr` backend
to call: under `local_backend("quickr")` a function containing a custom call
fails to compile with *does not support these primitives: custom_call*.

## When a custom call pays off

A custom call is opaque to XLA.
XLA cannot fuse it with the operations around it, so its operands and result
are written out to memory in full; [`gradient()`] cannot see into it; and it
only runs where a handler was registered.
A formula that anvl's operations can express -- however long -- is therefore
better left to them: XLA fuses it into a single pass over the data, and it
stays differentiable and portable.

A custom call pays off where that does not work:

- The work for one element is a **loop whose length depends on the element**:
  a series summed until it converges, a continued fraction, a root search,
  rejection sampling.
  StableHLO's only loop is a `while` over the whole array, so every element
  goes round it as often as the slowest one, and the whole state crosses the
  loop boundary on every trip.
  In C++, each element stops when it is done.
- A library already does the job.
  anvl's own linear algebra works this way: [`nv_chol()`], [`nv_qr()`] and
  [`nv_svd()`] call LAPACK on CPU and cuSOLVER on CUDA.

## The example: the Poisson upper tail

We will compute the upper tail of the Poisson distribution, $P(X > k)$ for
$X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$.
Computing it as one minus the lower tail fails as soon as the tail is small:

```{r}
1 - ppois(60, 10)
ppois(60, 10, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

R instead sums a series, starting from the density $d = P(X = k)$.
Where $\lambda \le k$, it sums the upper series
$$P(X > k) = d \left(\frac{\lambda}{k + 1} + \frac{\lambda^2}{(k + 1)(k + 2)} + \dots\right),$$
and where $\lambda > k$ the lower one, which gives $P(X < k)$ and so
$P(X > k) = 1 - P(X < k) - d$:
$$P(X < k) = d \left(\frac{k}{\lambda} + \frac{k (k - 1)}{\lambda^2} + \dots\right).$$
Each term is the previous one times a ratio below one, and the sum stops as
soon as the rest can no longer change it.
How soon that is depends on the element: $k = 1000$, $\lambda = 0.5$ needs 5
terms, $k = \lambda = 1000$ needs 273.

That is exactly the loop described above.
anvl's own [`nv_ppois()`] sums these series in a `nv_while()` over the whole
array, and it takes some 90 lines of carefully tuned anvl code -- unrolled
steps, rescaling to stay in range, freezing elements that have converged --
to make that fast.
The C++ version below is a plain loop of a dozen lines.
On our development machine, for a million elements with $\lambda$ between 1
and 150, the first call of a jitted [`nv_ppois()`] took 5.5 s, most of it
compiling, and later calls 1.3 s; the custom call took 0.5 s and 0.44 s, as a
single-threaded loop.

## Step 1: Write the handler

A custom call handler is a C++ function that receives one argument per
operand and one `Result<>` per result of the call, and returns an
`xla::ffi::Error`.
The buffers are already allocated by XLA; the handler only fills the results
in.

{pjrt} ships XLA's FFI headers in its `inst/include`, and the FFI API is
header-only, so `LinkingTo: pjrt` in a package -- or
`// [[Rcpp::depends(pjrt)]]` with `Rcpp::sourceCpp()`, as here -- is all that
is needed to compile against it.

```{Rcpp}
// [[Rcpp::plugins(cpp20)]]
// [[Rcpp::depends(pjrt)]]
#include <Rcpp.h>
#include <cfloat>
#include <cmath>
#include "xla/ffi/api/ffi.h"

using namespace xla::ffi;

// P(X > k) for X ~ Poisson(lambda), with k a whole number >= 0 and
// lambda > 0, from the same two series as R's ppois().
template <typename T>
static T ppois_upper(T k, T lambda) {
  if (std::isnan(k) || std::isnan(lambda)) return k + lambda;
  const T density = std::exp(k * std::log(lambda) - lambda - std::lgamma(k + 1));
  // lambda <= k: P(X > k) = density * (r1 + r1 r2 + ...), r_n = lambda / (k + n)
  // lambda > k:  P(X < k) = density * (r1 + r1 r2 + ...), r_n = (k - n + 1) / lambda
  const bool upper = lambda <= k;
  const T tol = (sizeof(T) == 4 ? FLT_EPSILON : DBL_EPSILON) / 2;
  T term = 1, sum = 0;
  for (int n = 1; n <= 100000; ++n) {
    const T r = upper ? lambda / (k + n) : (k - n + 1) / lambda;
    term *= r;
    // The ratios only shrink, so this term and all after it add up to at most
    // term / (1 - r). Stop as soon as that can no longer change the sum.
    if (term <= (1 - r) * sum * tol) break;
    sum += term;
  }
  return upper ? density * sum : 1 - density * (1 + sum);
}

// The actual work, once the element type is known.
template <typename T>
static Error ppois_upper_impl(AnyBuffer k, AnyBuffer lambda,
                              Result<AnyBuffer> out) {
  size_t n = out->element_count();
  if (k.element_count() != n || lambda.element_count() != n) {
    return Error::InvalidArgument("ppois_upper: operands must have the same size");
  }
  const T *kp = k.typed_data<T>();
  const T *lp = lambda.typed_data<T>();
  T *op = out->typed_data<T>();
  for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    op[i] = ppois_upper(kp[i], lp[i]);
  }
  return Error::Success();
}

// Dispatch on the dtype; f32 and f64 are what the loop is written for.
static Error do_ppois_upper(AnyBuffer k, AnyBuffer lambda,
                            Result<AnyBuffer> out) {
  DataType dt = k.element_type();
  if (lambda.element_type() != dt || out->element_type() != dt) {
    return Error::InvalidArgument("ppois_upper: operands and result must have "
                                  "the same dtype");
  }
  switch (dt) {
    case DataType::F32:
      return ppois_upper_impl<float>(k, lambda, out);
    case DataType::F64:
      return ppois_upper_impl<double>(k, lambda, out);
    default:
      return Error::InvalidArgument("ppois_upper: only f32 and f64 are supported");
  }
}

XLA_FFI_DEFINE_HANDLER(ppois_upper_handler, do_ppois_upper,
                       Ffi::Bind()
                           .Arg<AnyBuffer>()   // k
                           .Arg<AnyBuffer>()   // lambda
                           .Ret<AnyBuffer>()); // P(X > k)

// [[Rcpp::export]]
SEXP ppois_upper_handler_ptr() {
  return R_MakeExternalPtr((void *)ppois_upper_handler, R_NilValue, R_NilValue);
}
```

Three things are happening here:

- `ppois_upper_impl<T>()` is the implementation, and `do_ppois_upper()` picks
  the `T` at run time. `AnyBuffer` is a buffer of any dtype and rank, so the
  handler gets to look at `element_type()` and decide. The alternative is a
  statically typed `Buffer<DataType::F64>`, which pins the handler to one
  dtype and makes XLA reject everything else -- fine for a kernel that only
  ever runs in one precision, but not for one meant to be used from generic
  code.
- `XLA_FFI_DEFINE_HANDLER()` attaches the *binding specification* to it.
  Without it the runtime has no way to know that `do_ppois_upper` wants two
  operands and one result, in that order. The macro defines
  `ppois_upper_handler`, a plain function pointer.
- `ppois_upper_handler_ptr()` hands that pointer to R as an external pointer,
  which is what the registration function below expects. In a package this
  getter is unnecessary: declare the handler with
  `XLA_FFI_DEFINE_HANDLER_SYMBOL()` instead and look the resulting
  `extern "C"` symbol up with `getNativeSymbolInfo()`.

`AnyBuffer` moves the type checking from XLA into the handler, so the
handler has to do it: `typed_data<T>()` only asserts that `T` matches in a
debug build, and reinterprets the bytes otherwise.
Hence the explicit comparison of the three `element_type()`s and the
`default:` branch -- an `i32` operand comes back as
*ppois_upper: only f32 and f64 are supported* rather than as nonsense.

A handler may be called from XLA's worker threads, so it must not touch R's
C API (no allocation, no `Rf_error()`, no printing).
Report failures by returning an `Error` instead -- XLA aborts the execution
and {pjrt} re-raises it as an R error.

The loop above handles one element at a time on one thread, which is where
a production kernel goes further.
Binding `.Ctx<ThreadPool>()` hands the handler XLA's thread pool to split the
elements across, and the
[{highway}](https://github.com/louisaslett/highway) package, used through
`LinkingTo: highway`, provides Google's Highway library for SIMD: one kernel
that works on several elements per instruction, compiled for every
instruction set of the CPU and picked at run time.

## Step 2: Register it with PJRT

```{r}
pjrt::pjrt_register_custom_call(
  "mypkg_ppois_upper",
  list(cpu = ppois_upper_handler_ptr())
)
```

The target name is a process-global key, so prefix it with something
specific to your package -- `mypkg` stands in for its name here.
The second argument is one handler per platform, `"cpu"` (a synonym for
PJRT's own `"host"`) and `"cuda"`.
Platforms you leave out simply have no implementation: running the call
there aborts with *No FFI handler registered for `mypkg_ppois_upper`*.

Registration is *deferred*: if the plugin for a platform is not loaded yet,
the handler is queued and registered when it is.
Calling this in a package's `.onLoad()` is therefore fine, and you should
pass `.package = pkgname` there so that the handler is dropped again when
the package is unloaded.

## Step 3: Call it

[`nv_custom_call()`] takes the target name, the operands, and the dtype and
shape of each result as an [`AbstractArray()`].
anvl cannot infer the result types -- the handler decides them -- but
nothing forces you to write them out as literals: [`dtype()`] and [`shape()`]
of the operands are available at trace time, so a generic call reads

```{r}
library(anvl)
k <- nv_array(c(0, 3, 30, 60), dtype = "f64")
lambda <- nv_array(c(0.5, 10, 10, 10), dtype = "f64")
nv_custom_call(
  "mypkg_ppois_upper",
  k,
  lambda,
  output_types = AbstractArray(dtype(k), shape(k))
)
ppois(c(0, 3, 30, 60), c(0.5, 10, 10, 10), lower.tail = FALSE)
```

Wrapping that up gives an ordinary-looking `nv_*` function.
The handler requires both operands to have the same dtype and size, and
anvl's own API functions promote and broadcast before they compute, so the
wrapper does too, with the same helpers the built-in functions use:

```{r}
nv_ppois_upper <- function(k, lambda) {
  args <- do.call(nv_broadcast_arrays, nv_promote_to_common(k, lambda))
  nv_custom_call(
    "mypkg_ppois_upper",
    args[[1L]],
    args[[2L]],
    output_types = AbstractArray(dtype(args[[1L]]), shape(args[[1L]]))
  )
}

# a scalar lambda meets four counts
nv_ppois_upper(k, nv_scalar(10, dtype = "f64"))
```

It works the same inside a JIT-compiled function, where the custom call
becomes one op among the others -- and since the output types are derived
from the traced operands, one `jit()`ed function serves both dtypes:

```{r}
f <- jit(function(k, lambda) nv_sum(nv_ppois_upper(k, lambda)))
f(k, lambda)
f(nv_convert(k, "f32"), nv_convert(lambda, "f32"))
```

The handler computes the density through `lgamma()`, which loses a few
digits for large $k$; [`nv_ppois()`] uses a more careful formula there.
Matching R's last digits is a matter of numerics, not of the custom call.

The other arguments of `nv_custom_call()` worth knowing about:

- `attrs` is a named list of values the handler reads through
  `.Attr<T>("name")` or `.Attrs<Dictionary>()`. Strings, and numbers and
  logicals at the default data type of their category, are converted for
  you; pass a [`stablehlo::ScalarAttr()`] and friends to pin a data type.
- `operand_layouts` / `result_layouts` fix the memory layout XLA hands the
  handler -- see the next section.
- `aliases` says which operand's buffer each result is written into, so an
  in-place kernel does not force a copy. `aliases = 1L` on a single-result
  call hands the handler the same pointer for operand 1 and the result.
- `has_side_effect` keeps a call XLA would otherwise delete as unused. It
  defaults to `TRUE` exactly when `output_types` is `NULL`, which is how you
  write a printing or logging call; such a call returns its operands
  unchanged.

## Shapes and layouts: what the handler sees

anvl stores an array the way R does: in column-major order, the first axis
varying fastest.
XLA's arrays are row-major, the last axis varying fastest.
The two agree once every axis is reversed, so anvl hands XLA an array of R
shape $(d_1, \dots, d_n)$ as one of shape $(d_n, \dots, d_1)$, and the
bytes stay exactly as R has them.
A handler therefore sees

- `dimensions()` in reverse order: an R $3 \times 2$ matrix arrives with
  dimensions `{2, 3}`;
- the data in R's order: element `[i, j]` of that matrix at offset
  `(i - 1) + 3 * (j - 1)`, as `matrix()` lays it out and as LAPACK, written
  for Fortran, expects.

`operand_layouts` and `result_layouts` take one entry per operand or result:
its R axes, from the one varying fastest in memory to the one varying
slowest.
The default, `seq_len(n)` for an $n$-axis array, is R's own order, described
above.
A handler written for row-major (C order) buffers asks for
`rev(seq_len(n))` instead: XLA then rearranges the data before the call, and
element `[i, j]` sits at offset `2 * (i - 1) + (j - 1)`.
`dimensions()` stays the reversed R shape either way; the layout only
decides the order of the bytes.
Keep the default for a call that may see an array with an axis of size zero:
XLA's CPU compiler crashes compiling any other layout for one.

The Poisson handler treats its buffers as flat lists of elements, matched up
by position, so any layout works for it as long as all three buffers share
one -- which the default guarantees.

## Making it a primitive

`nv_custom_call()` is opaque to XLA, and therefore to {anvl}'s
differentiation: `gradient()` will not go through it.
It also shows up in a traced graph as a generic `custom_call` rather than
an operation with a name of its own.

Both are fixed the same way -- by giving the call its own primitive with a
pullback rule, exactly as in [Adding a Primitive](extending_primitive.html).
The dtype stays generic here too: the shape rule propagates whatever dtype
the operands were traced with, and the lowering rule is handed the
`output_types` that follow from it.
That rule reaches one level lower than `nv_custom_call()` does, emitting
[`stablehlo::hlo_custom_call()`] directly, because a rule is handed
`FuncValue`s rather than arrays.
Those speak XLA's order: their shapes are the R shapes reversed, and the
layouts are XLA's, which number the axes of that reversed shape from zero.
XLA's default layout, `n - 1` down to `0`, is R's column-major order:

```{r}
prim_ppois_upper <- new_primitive("ppois_upper", function(k, lambda) {
  graph_desc_add(self, list(k = k, lambda = lambda), infer_fn = function(k, lambda) {
    list(AbstractArray(dtype = dtype(k), shape = shape(k)))
  })[[1L]]
})

prim_ppois_upper[["stablehlo"]] <- function(k, lambda, output_types) {
  layout <- rev(seq_along(shape(k)) - 1L)
  list(stablehlo::hlo_custom_call(
    k,
    lambda,
    call_target_name = "mypkg_ppois_upper",
    api_version = 4L,
    has_side_effect = FALSE,
    output_types = output_types,
    operand_layouts = list(layout, layout),
    result_layouts = list(layout)
  ))
}

prim_ppois_upper[["pullback"]] <- rule_pullback(function(
  inputs,
  outputs,
  grads,
  params,
  required
) {
  k <- inputs[[1L]]
  lambda <- inputs[[2L]]
  list(
    # P(X > k) only changes where k passes a whole number
    if (required[[1L]]) nv_fill_like(k, 0),
    # d/dlambda P(X > k) = P(X = k)
    if (required[[2L]]) grads[[1L]] * nv_dpois(k, lambda)
  )
})
```

The pullback rule is ordinary anvl code: XLA runs the handler for the
values, and the gradient is computed from them by the operations the rule
emits.
Now the call differentiates, in either precision:

```{r}
g <- jit(gradient(function(k, lambda) nv_sum(prim_ppois_upper(k, lambda)), wrt = "lambda"))
g(k, lambda)
dpois(c(0, 3, 30, 60), c(0.5, 10, 10, 10))
g(nv_convert(k, "f32"), nv_convert(lambda, "f32"))
```

A real `nv_ppois_upper()` would then promote and broadcast its arguments as
above and call `prim_ppois_upper()` instead of `nv_custom_call()`: the
promotion belongs in the `nv_*` layer, the primitive takes the dtypes as
they come.

## Shipping this in a package

`Rcpp::sourceCpp()` keeps this article self-contained, but in a package you
would:

1. put the `.cpp` file in `src/`, declare the handler with
   `XLA_FFI_DEFINE_HANDLER_SYMBOL()`, and add `pjrt` to `LinkingTo:` and
   `C++20` to `SystemRequirements:`,
2. register it from `.onLoad()`, passing `.package = pkgname` so the handler
   goes away with the package:

   ```r
   .onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
     pjrt::pjrt_register_custom_call(
       "mypkg_ppois_upper",
       list(cpu = getNativeSymbolInfo("PpoisUpperHandler", PACKAGE = pkgname)$address),
       .package = pkgname
     )
   }
   ```

## Going to CUDA

Nothing on the R side changes for a GPU.
A `stablehlo.custom_call` names a *target*, not an implementation, and
`pjrt_register_custom_call()` already takes one handler per platform, so the
same `nv_ppois_upper(k, lambda)` runs the CUDA handler as soon as its
operands live on a CUDA device:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
k <- nv_array(c(0, 3, 30, 60), dtype = "f64", device = "cuda")
lambda <- nv_array(c(0.5, 10, 10, 10), dtype = "f64", device = "cuda")
nv_ppois_upper(k, lambda)
```

The kernel suits a GPU well: one thread per element, each running its own
loop.
The threads of a warp -- 32 on NVIDIA hardware -- still wait for the slowest
among them, but that is the slowest of 32 elements rather than of the whole
array.
On a slice of an A100, the million elements from above took 3 ms per call,
against 5 ms for [`nv_ppois()`], whose first call spent 4 s compiling.
What changes is the handler, and above all how it is built: R's build system
knows how to compile `.cpp`, not `.cu`.

### Share the per-element function

`ppois_upper()` is the same for both platforms, so move it into a header
that the CPU handler and the CUDA kernel both include.
Under `nvcc`, it has to be marked `__host__ __device__` to be callable from
the kernel; everything it calls -- `std::exp()`, `std::log()`,
`std::lgamma()`, `std::isnan()`, and `FLT_EPSILON` rather than
`std::numeric_limits` -- is available in device code too:

```c++
// src/ppois_upper.h -- included by the CPU handler and the CUDA kernel
#pragma once
#include <cfloat>
#include <cmath>

#ifdef __CUDACC__
#define MYPKG_HOST_DEVICE __host__ __device__
#else
#define MYPKG_HOST_DEVICE
#endif

template <typename T>
MYPKG_HOST_DEVICE T ppois_upper(T k, T lambda) {
  // ... the body from Step 1, unchanged
}
```

### Keep the kernel and the handler in separate files

Put the kernel in a `.cu` compiled by `nvcc`, and the FFI handler in a
`.cpp` compiled by R's ordinary C++ toolchain, with one `extern "C"`
launcher bridging them.
Typing the stream as `void *` at that boundary means the `.cpp` never
includes a CUDA header and the `.cu` never includes an XLA one -- which
matters, because `nvcc`'s C++ support trails the host compiler's.
This is the same split {pjrt} uses for its own CUDA handlers.

The kernel itself is a template, but `extern "C"` cannot be, so the `.cu`
exposes one launcher per supported dtype:

```c++
// src/ppois_upper_kernel.cu -- compiled by nvcc
#include <cuda_runtime.h>
#include "ppois_upper.h"

template <typename T>
__global__ void ppois_upper_kernel(const T *k, const T *lambda, T *out,
                                   size_t n) {
  size_t i = blockIdx.x * static_cast<size_t>(blockDim.x) + threadIdx.x;
  if (i < n) out[i] = ppois_upper(k[i], lambda[i]);
}

// Returns NULL on success, and CUDA's description of the error otherwise.
template <typename T>
static const char *launch(void *stream, const T *k, const T *lambda, T *out,
                          size_t n) {
  if (n == 0) return nullptr;  // a launch of zero blocks is itself an error
  const int threads = 256;
  const int blocks = static_cast<int>((n + threads - 1) / threads);
  ppois_upper_kernel<T><<<blocks, threads, 0, static_cast<cudaStream_t>(stream)>>>(
      k, lambda, out, n);
  cudaError_t err = cudaGetLastError();
  return err == cudaSuccess ? nullptr : cudaGetErrorString(err);
}

// The only symbols the rest of the package sees.
extern "C" const char *mypkg_launch_ppois_upper_f32(void *stream,
                                                    const float *k,
                                                    const float *lambda,
                                                    float *out, size_t n) {
  return launch<float>(stream, k, lambda, out, n);
}

extern "C" const char *mypkg_launch_ppois_upper_f64(void *stream,
                                                    const double *k,
                                                    const double *lambda,
                                                    double *out, size_t n) {
  return launch<double>(stream, k, lambda, out, n);
}
```

```c++
// src/ppois_upper_cuda.cpp -- compiled by R's C++ toolchain, no CUDA headers
#include <string>
#include "xla/ffi/api/ffi.h"

using namespace xla::ffi;

extern "C" const char *mypkg_launch_ppois_upper_f32(void *stream,
                                                    const float *k,
                                                    const float *lambda,
                                                    float *out, size_t n);
extern "C" const char *mypkg_launch_ppois_upper_f64(void *stream,
                                                    const double *k,
                                                    const double *lambda,
                                                    double *out, size_t n);

static Error do_ppois_upper_cuda(void *stream, AnyBuffer k, AnyBuffer lambda,
                                 Result<AnyBuffer> out) {
  size_t n = out->element_count();
  if (k.element_count() != n || lambda.element_count() != n) {
    return Error::InvalidArgument("ppois_upper: operands must have the same size");
  }
  DataType dt = k.element_type();
  if (lambda.element_type() != dt || out->element_type() != dt) {
    return Error::InvalidArgument("ppois_upper: operands and result must have "
                                  "the same dtype");
  }
  // these are *device* pointers; only the kernel may dereference them
  const char *err = nullptr;
  switch (dt) {
    case DataType::F32:
      err = mypkg_launch_ppois_upper_f32(stream, k.typed_data<float>(),
                                         lambda.typed_data<float>(),
                                         out->typed_data<float>(), n);
      break;
    case DataType::F64:
      err = mypkg_launch_ppois_upper_f64(stream, k.typed_data<double>(),
                                         lambda.typed_data<double>(),
                                         out->typed_data<double>(), n);
      break;
    default:
      return Error::InvalidArgument("ppois_upper: only f32 and f64 are supported");
  }
  if (err != nullptr) return Error::Internal(std::string("ppois_upper: ") + err);
  return Error::Success();
}

XLA_FFI_DEFINE_HANDLER_SYMBOL(PpoisUpperHandlerCuda, do_ppois_upper_cuda,
                              Ffi::Bind()
                                  .Ctx<PlatformStream<void *>>()
                                  .Arg<AnyBuffer>()
                                  .Arg<AnyBuffer>()
                                  .Ret<AnyBuffer>());
```

The binding gains one entry: `.Ctx<PlatformStream<void *>>()` puts the CUDA
stream XLA dispatched the op on in front of the buffers.
Everything the handler enqueues must go on *that* stream.

The handler returns as soon as the kernel is enqueued, so it can only report
what goes wrong with the launch itself -- which is why the launcher hands
back `cudaGetLastError()`.
Without that check, a kernel that never ran leaves its result unwritten, and
the error only surfaces, unrelated, at the next CUDA call.

### You do not need a system CUDA toolkit

On a machine with an NVIDIA GPU, `pjrt::install_pjrt()` installs the
[{pjrt.cuda}](https://github.com/r-xla/pjrt.cuda) R package along with the
CUDA plugin.
The first time it is loaded, {pjrt.cuda} downloads NVIDIA's CUDA
redistributables from PyPI and unpacks them, `nvcc` and every component's
headers included, into one tree under `pjrt.cuda::cuda_home()`:

```r
pjrt.cuda::bin_path("nvcc")          # nvcc and ptxas
pjrt.cuda::include_path("runtime")   # cuda_runtime.h, and the headers of the other components
pjrt.cuda::lib_path()                # all the .so files, libcudart.so.13 included
```

So everything the kernel above needs to compile and link is already on the
machine that runs the plugin, and a package can find it from R instead of
guessing at `/usr/local/cuda`.
Two caveats: {pjrt.cuda} is Linux only (x86_64 and aarch64), as is the CUDA
plugin, and it pins CUDA 13.3, the version the plugin is built against.
`PJRT_CUDA_R_PACKAGE` points {pjrt} at another package, but other versions
may not work with the plugin.

### Teaching `R CMD INSTALL` about `.cu`

R has no rule for `.cu`, so `src/Makevars` supplies one and lists every
object explicitly:

```make
CUDA_BIN = $(shell "$(R_HOME)/bin/Rscript" -e 'cat(pjrt.cuda::bin_path("nvcc"))')
CUDA_INC = $(shell "$(R_HOME)/bin/Rscript" -e 'cat(pjrt.cuda::include_path("runtime"))')
CUDA_LIB = $(shell "$(R_HOME)/bin/Rscript" -e 'cat(pjrt.cuda::lib_path())')

NVCC = $(CUDA_BIN)/nvcc

CXX_STD = CXX20
OBJECTS = ppois_upper.o ppois_upper_cuda.o ppois_upper_kernel.o
PKG_LIBS = -L$(CUDA_LIB) -l:libcudart.so.13 -Wl,-rpath,$(CUDA_LIB)

%.o: %.cu
	$(NVCC) -std=c++17 -O2 -arch=all-major -I$(CUDA_INC) -Xcompiler "$(CXXPICFLAGS)" -c $< -o $@
```

`nvcc` finds its own headers and tools relative to its `bin/`, so only the
include directory has to be named explicitly.
`-arch=all-major` has it compile machine code for every major GPU generation
it supports (`sm_75` and `sm_80` up to `sm_120` for CUDA 13), which a GPU of a
later minor generation, such as an `sm_86` card, runs as well.
Without it, `nvcc` only compiles machine code for `sm_75`, and every newer
GPU makes its driver compile the kernel from the intermediate PTX instead --
which a driver older than the `nvcc` that wrote the PTX refuses, with
*the provided PTX was compiled with an unsupported toolchain*.
The runtime comes as the versioned `libcudart.so.13` alone, without the
unversioned `libcudart.so` that `-lcudart` looks for, hence `-l:` with the
file name; the rpath lets the loaded package find it again.
A package meant to install on machines without a GPU wants a `configure` that
checks whether {pjrt.cuda} (or a system `nvcc`) is there at all, and generates
a `Makevars` without the CUDA objects when it is not.

### Registering both

`.onLoad()` then offers whichever handlers were actually built:

```r
symbol <- function(name, pkgname) {
  tryCatch(getNativeSymbolInfo(name, PACKAGE = pkgname)$address, error = function(e) NULL)
}

.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
  handlers <- list(
    cpu = symbol("PpoisUpperHandler", pkgname),
    cuda = symbol("PpoisUpperHandlerCuda", pkgname)
  )
  pjrt::pjrt_register_custom_call(
    "mypkg_ppois_upper",
    Filter(Negate(is.null), handlers),
    .package = pkgname
  )
}
```

Registering only `cpu` is not an error; a program that needs the missing
platform is what fails, with *No FFI handler registered for
`mypkg_ppois_upper`*.
